name: Carrington Bay Park
description:
Carrington Bay Park on Cortes Island covers 351 hectares (868 acres) of Crown land managed by the Strathcona Regional District since 2005. The trails are suitable for hiking and biking, with a trail to the lagoon takes about an hour through mature forest. Other marked trails branch off. Plan to arrive at low tide if possible.

The bay and lagoon, first surveyed in 1864, were named after Robert C. Carrington, draughtsman of the Hydrographic Office of the British Admiralty. Homesteaders settled in the bay early in the last century, and many were involved in logging and fishing. The lagoon and bay were used as a log dump and booming area.

Tent camping is permitted in the designated two areas near the log jam.

Access is from the trailhead on Carrington Bay Road.
keywords: hike, hiking, walk, bike, biking, cycling, forest, lagoon, camping, tenting, nature

name: Children's Forest
description:
The Children's Forest lands, adjacent to Carrington Lagoon, are currently under negotiation for purchase from Mosaic Forest Management to be held in trust for the children of Cortes in perpetuity. These ecologically significant lands contain provincially designated sensitive riparian, wetland, herbaceous, woodland and old-growth ecosystems.

Trails are accessed from Carrington Bay Road and range from 1.5 to 4 hours. Trail maps are posted at most junctions.

Access is from the trailhead on Carrington Bay Road.

Photo Christine Robinson

name: Easter Bluff Trail
description:
The Easter Bluff trail lies within the Linnaea Farm's protected land covenant - a sensitive ecosystem. To ensure its protection, stay on the trail; no fires or camping are permitted.

The steep and rocky trail will take you up to spectacular views to the west and the south. It is moderately difficult, with a 30-minute ascent to the top.

Access is from a small parking area on Cortes Bay Road, halfway between Manzanita and Seaford roads.

name: Katimavik Trail
description:
The Katimavik Trail connects Kw'as Park (near the "Serge" Narrows Bridge between Hague and Gunflint lakes) with the Easter Bluff Trail near Cortes Bay.

It opened in spring 2001. The trail was named to honour a Katimavik youth crew that built and cleared the route through rough terrain.

The standalone Katimavik Trail segment takes about 45 minutes to walk. As part of the combined Kw'as Park, Katimavik and Easter Bluff Trail, it forms an out-and-back route measuring roughly 7.6 km, with an average completion time of about 2 hours and 19 minutes.

Generally rated as moderately challenging, the route passes through forested and uneven terrain.

Access is from Bartholomew Road, just opposite the Easter Bluff trail, or from Kw'as Park near the "Serge" Narrows Bridge.

name: Ha'thayim von Donop Trails
description:
Three main hiking trails are user-maintained and the most rugged on Cortes. The 6 km (return) Von Donop trail descends to the inlet. The moderately challenging Norway Loop trail (6.1 km) begins there, offering views of the Von Donop and Squirrel Cove lagoons. The Squirrel Cove trail starts at the northwest end of the cove (2.6 km return) and ends at the lagoon where the other trails join. Large sword ferns sometimes obscure this trail, and blowdowns may be encountered on all trails.

This park is accessible from Von Donop Inlet and Squirrel Cove trailhead connected via a 5 km rugged trail system.
keywords: hike, hiking, rugged, challenging, forest, lagoon, inlet, squirrel cove, norway loop, wilderness

name: Ha'thayim Marine Park
description:
Ha'thayim Marine Park is a popular anchorage for boaters, with a long, sheltered inlet at the island's northwestern tip. Ha'thayim is the Coast Salish name for the area.
Three main hiking trails are user-maintained and the most rugged on Cortes. 
The 6 km (return) Von Donop trail descends to the base of the inlet. 
The moderately challenging Norway Loop trail (6.1 km) begins there, offering views of Von Donop and Squirrel Cove lagoons. 
The Squirrel Cove trail starts at the northwest end of the cove (2.6 km return) and ends at the lagoon where the other trails join. 
Large sword ferns sometimes obscure this trail, and blowdowns may be encountered on all trails.

There are no designated campsites at this park; however, random wilderness camping is allowed. 

No facilities are provided. This park is accessible year-round, and there is no winter camping fee. Please practise "Leave No Trace" camping ethics.

Access is from the Von Donop Inlet and a trail that starts in Carrington Bay Park.

name: Hank's Beach Trail
description:
Hank's Beach Forest Conservation Park is managed by the Strathcona Regional District (SRD). Two easy, parallel forest walks lead to a popular beach and picnic spot named after homesteader Henry Herrewig (Hank), who was granted the Crown Land in 1922.

From the beach, looking east, are views of the majestic mainland mountains; to the south, the Twin Islands; and to the west, Vancouver Island. Access to a longer beach to the west is also available at low tide.

Access is from a small parking area and trailhead on Bartholomew Road.
keywords: easy walk, walk, hike, hiking, forest, beach, picnic, family, kids, view, homestead history

name: Kw'as Park
description:
An extensive network of hiking-only (no biking allowed) trails is located in Kw'as Park, managed by the Strathcona Regional District. The park is a 70-hectare (173-acre) forested area nestled between Hague and Gunflint lakes. The trails traverse distinct ecosystems, including old-growth and mature second-growth cedar and Douglas fir forests. Evidence of logging is visible along the trails near Gunflint Lake. High, rocky bluffs, adorned with pines, arbutus, and manzanita, run parallel to the small creek that connects the two lakes. The Swim Rock trail leads to a popular swimming and picnicking spot on Hague Lake. SRD Trail Guides and additional trail information for some of the trails are available at the Museum.

Trails near Gunflint Lake show signs of logging.  Rocky bluffs with pines, arbutus, and manzanita run parallel to a creek connecting Hague and Gunflint lakes. The Swim Rock trail leads to popular swimming and picnicking spots on Hague Lake. Trail guides are available at the Museum.

Access from the trailheads located west of the motel and at the end of Kw'as Road.

name: Mansons Landing Park
description:
Mansons Landing Provincial Park, established in 1974 for day use, borders the white-sand beach of Hague Lake and the Mansons lagoon. A public wharf provides boaters with access.

Indigenous people gathered and dried shellfish here in summer, leaving behind a shell midden as evidence of long-term harvesting. In the late 1800s, Mike Manson emigrated from Scotland to Cortes Island, and with his brother John established here a wharf, trading post, lodge, post office and school. The area now bears his name, and many of his descendants still live on the island.

Access is from a parking lot at Mansons Lagoon at the bottom of Sutil Point Road.

name: School-to-Sea Trail
description:
This easy School-to-Sea trail connects the Cortes Island Public School on Beesley Road to the parking area at Manson's Lagoon. The trail takes you through the forest and along the bluff down to the ocean and the lagoon. A booklet created by the students provides information about the flora and fauna of the trail, which is marked by numbered posts.

Access: Left side of the soccer field behind the public school or from the parking lot at Manson's Lagoon.

name: Siskin Forest Trails
description:
Siskin Forest Park is a 13-hectare (32-acre) area donated by the Renewal Land Company to the Strathcona Regional District (SRD), which oversees the Siskin Lane Conservation Area's trail network that weaves through the surrounding residential properties.

Hiking, cycling, and horseback riding are allowed on the trails, which include some rough terrain. Fires are prohibited at all times. SRD trail guides and additional trail information for some of the trails are available at the Museum.

Access from trailheads on the left side of Cemetery Road, at Sutil Point Road, and at the end of Hayes Road.

name: Smelt Bay Park
description:
Smelt Bay is a popular, kid-friendly spot for walking, picnicking, swimming, sunsets, interesting tide pools and boulders at low tide, and a name chosen for the thousands of capelin fish (smelt) that used to spawn along the shore in the fall.

The beach begins at the base of Smelt Bay Road, with some areas sandy and others rocky. At very low tide, you can walk around Sutil Point to Moon Beach near Hollyhock with proper footwear, water, and a snack. Watch out for the quickly coming tide.

Access from a small parking area at the beach and at the end of Smelt Bay Rd.

name: Whaletown Commons
description:
After years of community involvement, the Strathcona Regional District purchased the 70 acres of Whaletown Commons in 2014 as a dedicated park space. The park's network of easy hiking trails (.5 to 1.5 hours) runs adjacent to Whaletown Creek, a salmon-bearing stream with a lush riparian zone and a few old-growth trees.

It is an important wildlife corridor through the area.

Access from the north side of Whaletown Road, adjacent to Firehall #2.

name: Green Mountain Trail
description:
Green Mountain trail offers stunning views to the west after hiking up a short distance along a rugged trail.

One section is roped off, so consider this if you find steep areas challenging. There is a loop at the top leading to a bench. This route is best enjoyed on clear days.

name: Hague Lake Beach
description:
The white sand beach at Hague Lake, part of Mansons Landing Provincial Park since 1974, was shaped by glaciers. It's a popular summer destination because the beach has a gentle slope towards the lake. During low tides, a trail along the lagoon connects to the beach via the park road.

A parking lot with pit toilets and an information board is located opposite the Hague Lake beach entrance. The park is a day-use area. Camping and fires are not allowed. Dogs are permitted on a leash only.

Access from a parking lot is cut into the woods opposite the Hague Lake's beach entrance.

name: Hank's Beach
description:
Hank's Beach Forest Conservation Park, managed by the Strathcona Regional District, offers two easy forest walks leading to a popular beach and picnic spot named after homesteader Henry Herrewig ("Hank"), granted Crown Land in 1922.

From the beach, you can see the mainland mountains, Twin Islands to the south, and Vancouver Island to the west. A wider beach is accessible at low tide.

name: Mansons Landing Park Water Access
description:
Mansons Landing Provincial Park, established in 1974 for day use, broadens marine park experiences in the Northern Gulf Islands. It borders Hague Lake's white sand beach and Mansons Landing Park's sandy spit and beach, with brackish lagoon waters. A public wharf outside the lagoon offers boaters access.

The spit is a fragile ecosystem, so stay on the trails. You can launch your kayaks or boats from the lagoon side.

Ample parking is available at the end of Mansons Road.

name: Smelt Bay Beach
description:
The beach at Smelt Bay is a popular spot for walking, picnicking, swimming, and watching sunset. It is also our island's most kid-friendly beach. An incredible myriad of boulders and tide pools emerges at low tide, waiting to be explored.

Access to the beach begins at the bottom of the Smelt Bay Road hill, continuing to the Provincial Park parking lot. Some portions of the beach are sandy, others rocky. At an extremely low tide, it is possible to walk all the way around Sutil Point to Moon Beach near Hollyhock (with proper footwear, water and a snack). But be aware of the incoming tide that rushes in quickly across the flats.

The present-day name Smelt Bay was chosen for the thousands of capelin fish (smelt) spawning along the shore in the fall.

description:

You can walk to Smelt Bay (left) or Manson's Park (right) from here, but do so at low tide, as some beach areas may be difficult to walk on.

name: Squirrel Cove Post Office
description:
The Squirrel Cove post office first opened in 1916 in a small building near the wharf. As no roads connected Squirrel Cove to the other operating post offices, it was important to the many people who lived in this area. It was run by the Forrest family for the next 66 years when the post office was closed. For the next 24 years the residents had to travel either to post offices in Mansons Landing or Whaletown to receive their mail. Finally in 2006, the Squirrel Cove post office reopened in the Squirrel Cove General Store, its current location.

name: Chamadaska Post Office
description:
Chamadaska Post Office opened September 15, 1910. The island, named in 1792 as Marina Island, was for some time renamed to Mary Island, but that caused confusion as there were already at least three Mary islands and one Merry Island, so later (June 30, 1906) it was renamed back to the original name, Marina Island. 

Chamadaska might refer to the "whale route" or "passage for whales" (information provided March 2004 by Cortes Island resident M. Abelson, in turn relayed from M. Hansen, whose family have lived on Cortes Island for 5 or more generations)

The post office was served by the Union steamships. The post office was officially closed on June 30, 1923.

name: First Squirrel Cove Post Office
description:
Squirrel Cove post office on Cortes Island has a rare history, being the only location on the west cost of B.C. were a post office was opened, ran for 66 years, was then closed for 24 years and then re-opened. 

The original post office opened on February 1, 1916, and was run by the Forrest family who ran mail service for 66 years until the post office closed. The mail was brought by the Forrest family in their 16-foot rowboat and picked up from the Union steamship that stopped in the Lewis Channel as the Squirrel Cove was too small for them.

The post office is now Located in the Squirrel Cove General Store.

name: Museum & Archives
description:

The museum is open year-round, and its shop features the works of local authors, artists, and craftspeople. Admission is free. Donations are appreciated.
more_details:
The Cortes Island Museum building began in 1946 as a family store at the head of Manson's Landing dock. A nearby mill in the lagoon supplied the lumber. When the area became a provincial park in 1974, the store was allowed to continue operating until 1991.
May Ellingsen, a granddaughter of Mike Manson, dreamed of establishing a museum on Cortes. In the late 1920s, she began diligently collecting photographs, stories and papers from early homesteader families. She also collected papers and catalogues from Cortes businesses and organizations, as well as newspaper articles about the island.
Read more about museum's history on the website, www.cortesmuseum.com/about-us/mission-vision/.

It was once home to the Linnaea School, which offered a rich programme of creative, nature-based, global, and alternative learning for hundreds of students over 23 years, and to the Linnaea Ecological Gardening Program, a small-scale organic gardening and farming program that has imparted values and practical skills in ecological land stewardship since 1987.

Key features:
- The bark: It has a highly distinctive, vertically stringy bark that tears away in long fibrous strips.
- The base: Mature western redcedars develop a massively flared, fluted, and buttressed trunk at the base.
- The habitat: The surrounding lush understory filled with sword ferns is a textbook example of an old-growth, moist temperate rainforest ecosystem in the Pacific Northwest, where these giants thrive.

Known as the "Tree of Life" by Indigenous coastal peoples, these magnificent trees are exceptionally rot-resistant and can live to be well over 1,000 years old.
